question.prompt:
A square floor is tiled with congruent square tiles. The tiles on the two diagonals of the floor are black. The rest of the tiles are white. If there are \(101\) black tiles, then the total number of tiles is

[Figure 1](figures/1992_AMC_12_Q08_question_fig1.svg)

solutions.explanation:
Let \(n\) be the positive integer number of tiles along each side of the floor. Each diagonal passes through one tile in each row, so each diagonal contributes \(n\) tiles. We must check whether adding these two counts counts any tile twice.

If \(n\) is even, the diagonals meet at a grid vertex in the center, and their tile lists have no tile in common. There would be \(2n\) black tiles, an even number, so this cannot give \(101\).

If \(n\) is odd, the diagonals pass through the same central tile. This is their only shared tile: in row \(r\), the two diagonal tiles are in columns \(r\) and \(n+1-r\), which agree only in the middle row. Subtracting the one duplicate gives
\[
2n-1=101,
\qquad n=51.
\]
This value is odd, as required. There are \(51\) rows of \(51\) tiles, so the total is
\[
51\cdot51=\boxed{2601},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
solutions.title: Count the diagonals and correct the overlap
